subject: Estimation of direct, indirect and total effects, and some other questions

messages.author: 1eec5310e38e5422
messages.subject: Estimation of direct, indirect and total effects, and some other questions
parts:
Hello,

I have a data set with multiple dependent variables and multiple independent variables. In addition, the data is nested: there are multiple patches, and within each patch several individuals. The dependent variables were measured at the individual level, but independent variables were measured both at the individual and at the patch level. Those independent variables that were measured at the individual level may also be dependent on the independent variables that were measured at the patch level. 
All my variables are continuous. The dependent variables are all supposed to represent the same phenomena, but when I tried creating a latent variables out of them it gave a poor fit (maybe because some of the measured variables are inverse to one another).
Though I don't have any latent variables, I thought that due to the complex structure of the data lavaan would be appropriate to use. I'd be happy to hear if this is not accurate and there are other packages that are more recommended for such a design.
My questions are:
1. Would it be more appropriate to account for the nestedness of the data by using a multilevel model in lavaan and using the patches as clusters, or to use lavaan.survey?
2. What are the appropriate fit indices to look at for multilevel models?
3. Are there any recommended packages for plotting lavaan models? Semplot works poorly when there are many variables and connections.
4. Is there an efficient way to estimate direct, indirect and total effects in lavaan? I know one can add equations in the syntax to do that, but for complex models this can be quite tedious. 

Thanks for your help and attention,
Efrat

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Estimation of direct, indirect and total effects, and some other questions
parts: 1. Would it be more appropriate to account for the nestedness of the data by using a multilevel model in lavaan and using the patches as clusters, or to use lavaan.survey?

lavaan.survey() only corrects SEs and tests for clustering in a level-1 model (also available in lavaan() now, if you specify a cluster= variable for a single-level model).  You have Level-2 hypotheses (a patch-level IV predicts the patch-level component of an individual-level IV), so MLSEM seems more appropriate.
2. What are the appropriate fit indices to look at for multilevel models?
All the same fit indices are available, but it is recommended to evaluate fit at each level separately.  SRMRs are available at each level of analysis.
3. Are there any recommended packages for plotting lavaan models? Semplot works poorly when there are many variables and connections.
And I think it only plots MLSEMs from Mplus output; not sure about OpenMx or lavaan yet.
4. Is there an efficient way to estimate direct, indirect and total effects in lavaan? I know one can add equations in the syntax to do that, but for complex models this can be quite tedious.

No, but you can check to see if you missed any by multiplying the beta matrix (at either level) against itself 2, then 3, then ... p-1 times (the maximum number of sequential causal links).

B <- lavInspect(fit, "est")[[1]]$beta # level-1 beta
B %*% B        # 2-path indirect effects
B %*% B %*% B  # 3-path indirect effects


By the time you get a product full of zeros, you won't have any more indirect effects of higher order.  Each nonzero cell is the point estimate for an indirect effect whose path you can trace from the predictor (column variable) to the outcome (row variable).  To obtain the delta-method SEs, you can check that each nonzero cell in each product is represented in your model syntax.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Estimation of direct, indirect and total effects, and some other questions
parts: What I am unsure about is whether I need to specify the level-1 DVs in the level-2 equation?

Every level-1 variable has a level-2 component (i.e., the cluster means) whose variance can only be modeled at level 2.  If you have no hypotheses about it, you could just allow it to covary with everything else at level 2, but it should be accounted for in your syntax
should I parameterize them with the same path coefficients as they have in the level-1 equation, or with new ones?

Are you asking whether they need to be equal across levels?  No, process across levels can look very different.  Level-1 and -2 models do not have to have the same form, nor equal estimates of any parameters that are in both models.  But the data must be modeled (i.e., level-1 variables have level-2 components, period).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Dear Terrance and all,

Thank you for your reply. 
I am still unsure how to specify the model. I will try to illustrate with a simplified example:
Say that I want to study factors that affect students' grades in 3 subjects (Y1, Y2 and Y3). The explanatory variables I will be testing have been measured in two levels: schools, and classes within those schools. For the schools I measured 3 variables (X1, X2 and X3), and for the classes I measured another three variables (M1, M2 and M3).

The following illustration shows the hypothesized paths from the conceptual model:



Which of the two following syntax is appropriate? :

Option 1:

m1 <- '
Level: 1
Y1 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
Y2 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
Y3 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
M3 ~ M1 + M2

Level: 2
Y1 ~ X1 + X2 + X3
Y2 ~ X1 + X2 + X3 
Y3 ~ X1 + X2 + X3   
M1 ~ X1 + X2 + X3 
M2 ~ X1 + X2 + X3 
M3 ~ X1 + X2 + X3 
'

Option 2:

m2 <- '
Level: 1
Y1 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
Y2 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
Y3 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
M3 ~ M1 + M2

Level: 2
Y1 ~ X1 + X2 + X3 +  M1 + M2 + M3
Y2 ~ X1 + X2 + X3  +  M1 + M2 + M3
Y3 ~ X1 + X2 + X3   +  M1 + M2 + M3
M1 ~ X1 + X2 + X3  
M2 ~ X1 + X2 + X3 
M3 ~ X1 + X2 + X3  + M2 + M3
'

Thanks in advance,
Efrat

parts: Option 2 is the most comprehension.  It models the same effects at the school-mean level (Level 2) as at the class level (Level 1), but Level 2 also includes the effects of Level-2 predictors (Xs) on the Level-2 components of all 6 Level-1 variables.

So if I go with option 2 and have the effects of level-2 variables on the level-1 predictors, what would be the appropriate way to parameterize the path coefficients - same in both levels, or different for each level?
